teaching.task: # Year 12 Physics M5 V03: Height, flight time and landing velocity. What determines height, flight time and landing velocity at the launch level? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Start with the height. At the top, the vertical velocity is zero, and we don't need to know when that happens. So choose the equation without time in it, v squared equals u squared plus two a s, written for the vertical column. Put in v y equals zero and a y equals minus g, and it rearranges to the height above the launch point: H equals u y squared over two g. Only the vertical component appears. Moving sideways doesn't help the ball climb at all. For our ball, u y is twenty-five sin fifty, about nineteen point one five metres per second. Squared, that's about three hundred and sixty-seven. Divide by two times nine point eight, which is nineteen point six, and the maximum height is about eighteen point seven metres above the launch point. Now the flight time. The ball lands when it's back at its launch level, so its vertical displacement is zero. Write s equals u t plus a half a t squared for the vertical column, and set it to zero: u y t minus four point nine t squared equals zero. Take out a factor of t, and there are two answers. t equals zero is the moment of launch, when the ball was also at that level, so that's not the one we want. The other is t equals two u y over g.

- **No human figures.**

  (a) H is measured above the launch point (the barrel tip), taken as level with the landing ground (v02 author note a).

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "What determines height, flight time and landing velocity at the launch level?" The answer: the vertical component u_y alone sets the height (through u_y²) and the time (through u_y), because gravity brings u_y to zero and back; the horizontal component is untouched, so the landing velocity is the launch velocity reflected; all of this needs landing at the launch level.
- **Opening frame (v02 handoff).** v02's final frame (see v02 "Final frame"): launcher at 50° on level ground, the rising half drawn, the ball at the peak with only its teal arrow "16.1 m s⁻¹", the falling half dashed, brackets "?" (height), "t = ?" (time) and a dashed landing arrow "v = ?", ledger with u_x = 16.1 and u_y = 19.2 m s⁻¹. Scene 1 speaks over it; the three "?" become the scene order (height 2, 3; time 4, 5; landing 6).
- **Prediction (new): landing speed faster, slower or the same?** A natural split of intuitions ("gravity speeds it up", "it slows down in the air"); the answer in scene 6 (same speed, mirrored direction) follows from the components, not from a rule.
- **Height (site worked example 2(a) and the "Apply 6 marks" step 4).** The equation without t is chosen because the time isn't needed (a choice explained, not announced). H is the height above the launch point (site key formula wording).
- **Flight time (site lesson 2 derivation and "Apply 6 marks" step 3; pack trap "the root t = 0 is launch, not landing").** s_y = 0 is factorised on screen; both roots are kept visible and t = 0 is labelled "launch". The doubling is explained causally (gravity removes and restores u_y at the same rate), not just asserted as symmetry.
- **Landing velocity (route "track signed vertical velocity and unchanged horizontal velocity").** v_y is tracked with its sign through the flight on a small v_y against t line beside the stage (kit: `VelocityTimeGraph`, reconfigured to 25 m s⁻¹ at 50°, g = 9.8; pack section 5): it falls in a straight line from +19.15 through zero at 1.95 s to −19.15 at 3.91 s, while the teal v_x line stays flat at 16.07.

- **Relationships and the site correction (pack section 3; `../site-corrections-phys-y12.md` records 1 and 2).** Site lesson 2's "Apply 6 marks" answer says "All three grow with the square of the launch speed". The design teaches the corrected relationship: at a fixed angle, T is proportional to u (doubling u doubles T) and H to u² (doubling u gives four times H). Shown with the 25 → 50 m s⁻¹ case (T 3.91 → 7.82 s; H 18.7 → 74.9 m, screen only). The site's text is not quoted to learners.

## Visual upgrade (Revision 3)

The Revision 2 visual upgrade is already written into each scene's Visual line (anchor, simulation, colour roles, hand tags, framed answers). This section tops the design up to the checklist used for Year 11 Physics, Biology and Chemistry, and applies root rules R1 to R4 (`../checks/root-acceptance-y11-upgrade-12-nov.md`). Where a scene has an "Upgrade (Revision 3)" paragraph, it adds to the Visual and wins wherever the two differ. No narration line changed.

- **Board stages.** (A) last time's frame: the launcher, the path and the three questions, scene 1 (about 36 s); (B) the ledger large beside the stage, scene 2 (about 34 s); (C) the full-width calculation layout, scene 3 (about 22 s); (D) the full-width factorising stage with the launch-level strip, scene 4 (about 33 s); (E) the stage with the coupled velocity graph, scene 5 (about 32 s); (F) the push to the landing point and its triangle, then the pull back for the range, scenes 6 and 7 (about 48 s); (G) the two boxed forms and the launch-speed slider, scene 8 (about 41 s); (H) the stage with the cliff condition, scene 9 (about 20 s); (I) the mirror and the memory card, scene 10 (about 27 s); question and feedback cards; the handoff; the notes board. No set-up runs past about 48 s, so no cut was needed.
- **Simulation engines (`src/explainer/sims/`).** The flights run on the field motion engine (`field-motion.ts`, a `uniform` field with ax = 0 and ay = −9.8) and are drawn with `FieldMotionView` (trail, strobe images, velocity arrows with components, ground line) on one `useMotionTime` clock. Every clock value, strobe position, arrow length and readout is read from `stateAt` of that run, so the picture and the numbers cannot disagree. This replaces the physics of v01's kit gap 1 (the strobe projectile stage). The scene 5 flight (25 m s⁻¹ at 50°) drives the stage ball, the graph dot and the readouts "t", "v_y" and "v_x" from one `stateAt`, so v_y passes through zero exactly at the peak. The scene 8 slider is a set of runs from 25 to 50 m s⁻¹ at 50°; "T" and "H" are read from each run.
- **Answer frames and mistakes (root rule R1).** Every answer sits in a dark-ink frame with an ink tick. Every mistake takes a slate scribble and a slate hand tag; "not possible" takes a slate cross. This overrides any red crossing, strike, chip or tag in the Visual lines and in "Colour roles". Red and green keep only their subject meanings.
- **Solid ink (root rule R2).** The opening frame and the final frame are drawn solid in full ink wherever a line calls part of them "faint", "ghost", "pale", "dim" or "grey", so both sides of each join match. Text a student must read is never faint: an earlier row that "dims" stays solid at a smaller size, and an earlier path that "stays faint" is a thin solid line in its role colour.
- **No coded drawings of real objects.** Apparatus and real objects are painted plates (the `y12p-` set or existing plates), scaled uniformly and never stretched. Exam-style outlines (ground, walls, cliffs, bench edges), vectors, field lines, graphs and circuit symbols stay coded, as root decision 3 for this course records.
- **No video numbers on screen.** Where a Visual line tags something with a video code, the on-screen words say "last time", "an earlier video" or "next time". Video codes in this document are notes for the builder.
- **Question cards.** Each attempt card arrives whole (sentences 38 px) with a picture from its first frame. The picture is answer-free: nothing on it can be counted, measured or read off to get the answer. Method aids (ledgers, formula strips, memory cards) are hidden while a countdown runs; every supplied value and condition stays on the card. Each feedback scene keeps a navy givens strip from its first frame.
- **Notes scene.** Five one-line bullets (95 characters or fewer, 34 px, role colours), the framed memory card beside them, and a notes scene of 45 s in all.

scenes.teachingReason: So at equal levels, the vertical component sets the height and the flight time, and the horizontal component turns that time into a range: sixty-two point eight metres for our ball. Now launch it at forty degrees instead, at the same speed. It doesn't go as high, and it comes down sooner, yet it lands in exactly the same spot. Why? That's next.
